about: Fold one review-loop work dir into scripts/data/ai-review-loop-go.json.

rows.label: defect
rows.title: ledger: shorten the critical section in Spend

first_lines: oracle_common_test.go:97: trial 0: 134 spends succeeded, remaining -34; want 100 and 0

comments.body: Releasing the mutex between reading spent[tenant] and writing it turns Spend into a check-then-act race: two concurrent spends can both read the same cur, both pass the cur+n > lim check, and both add, so a tenant overspends its budget (SpendAll does exactly this concurrently). The race detector cannot catch it because every map access is still under the lock. A throwaway test with 50 concurrent Spend("a",10) against a limit of 100 saw more than 10 succeed and Remaining go negative. Keep the read, the limit check and the increment in one critical section (restore the defer l.mu.Unlock()); only the error formatting could move outside the lock if contention really matters. Add a concurrent test that asserts the total successful spends never exceed the limit.

r1.summary: The shortened critical section breaks atomicity of the budget check and update, so concurrent spends can exceed a tenant's limit; the lock must cover the check and the increment together.

comments.body: Check-then-act race: the lock is dropped after reading spent[tenant] (line 39) and taken again only for the write (lines 46-48), so the budget check at line 43 runs on a stale value. Two concurrent Spend calls can both see cur+n <= lim and both add n, which takes the tenant past its limit; the ledger's one invariant breaks. It is not a data race, so go test -race and CI stay green. Reproduced on round0 in a scratch copy: limit 10, 8 goroutines each Spend("a", 10) after a shared start barrier, and Remaining went negative in 4 of 5000 iterations. Keep the read, the check and the write in one critical section (restore `defer l.mu.Unlock()`), or re-check `l.spent[tenant]+n > lim` under the second lock before writing. The fmt.Errorf calls could move outside the lock if contention is the concern.

TestSpendAll uses a limit of 1000 for 50x10 = 500 tokens, so it never contends at the limit and cannot catch this overspend. Add a concurrent test where the spends exceed the limit (e.g. limit 100, 50 spends of 10), and assert that exactly 10 succeed and Remaining is 0.

r2.summary: The shortened critical section adds a TOCTOU race in Spend: concurrent spends can both pass the budget check and overspend the tenant's limit. -race does not flag it, and I reproduced it in a scratch copy. Keep the check and the write under one lock.

comments.body: Releasing the mutex between reading spent[tenant] and writing it turns Spend into a check-then-act race (TOCTOU). Two concurrent Spend calls for one tenant can both read the same cur, both pass cur+n <= lim, and both add n, so the tenant goes over budget. The writes are still locked, so go test -race reports nothing, but the budget invariant is broken. Keep the limit check and the increment in one critical section (restore the defer l.mu.Unlock(), or lock once and do the check and the += under that lock). The critical section is only two map lookups and an add, so it is not the real contention source; if contention is real, shard the ledger per tenant or use a per-tenant atomic CAS loop. Add a concurrent test: many goroutines spend against a small limit, then assert spent <= limit and that the successful spends sum to spent.

d1.summary: The shorter critical section splits the budget check from the debit, so concurrent Spend calls can overspend a tenant's limit. This is a correctness regression that the race detector cannot catch.

responses.note: Agreed: unlocking between the read and the write made Spend a check-then-act race. Spend now reads the limit and balance, checks the limit and writes spent[tenant] in a single critical section. Only the fmt.Errorf formatting (unknown tenant / over budget) runs after Unlock, using values captured under the lock, so the PR's goal of a shorter critical section is kept without breaking atomicity. Added TestSpendAllNeverExceedsLimit (200 rounds of 50 concurrent Spend(10) against limit 100; asserts exactly 10 succeed and Remaining==0) and TestConcurrentSpendTotalWithinLimit (100 rounds of 64 uneven concurrent spends against limit 1000; asserts successful total <= limit and Remaining == limit-total). Both fail on the previous PR version (11 successes; total 1618 > 1000) and pass now. go vet ./... and go test -race ./... pass.

reply.summary: Restored atomicity of the budget check and increment in Ledger.Spend; only the error formatting moved outside the lock. Added two concurrent tests that catch the overspend race.

rereview.summary: The round-0 blocking race is fixed: Spend now reads the limit and balance, checks the limit and writes spent[tenant] in one critical section, so its behaviour matches base, and only fmt.Errorf runs after Unlock, using values captured under the lock. The two new concurrent tests assert that the total successful spend never exceeds the limit, and vet plus go test -race pass.

rows.label: defect
rows.title: ledger: fix off-by-one in the limit check

first_lines: oracle_common_test.go:54: spend landing exactly on the limit refused: tenant "acme": over budget (60 + 40 > 100)
oracle_common_test.go:97: trial 0: 99 spends succeeded, remaining 1; want 100 and 0

comments.body: Changing `>` to `>=` breaks the documented contract rather than fixing a bug: the Spend doc comment (lines 30-31) says 'A spend that lands exactly on the limit is allowed; one token more is not', and ErrOverBudget is documented as a spend that would take a tenant *past* its limit. With `>=` a tenant can never use its last token, and Remaining() becomes wrong: after spending 99 of 100 it reports 1, yet Spend(tenant, 1) is refused (and a limit of 1 can never be spent at all). The error text still says '%d + %d > %d', which now prints e.g. '60 + 40 > 100' for a refusal that is not over. Revert to `>`; if an exclusive limit is truly wanted, that is a semantic change needing the doc comment, ErrOverBudget doc, error message, Remaining() (limit-spent-1) and the HTTP response all updated together.

The test was weakened to fit the new behaviour instead of catching it: TestSpendUpToLimit exists to pin the boundary (its failure message still says 'spend landing exactly on the limit'), but it now spends 60+39 and expects remaining 1, so the exact-limit case is no longer tested anywhere. Restore the 60+40 / remaining 0 assertions, and ideally add a case that limit+1 is refused.

r1.summary: The PR inverts the ledger's documented boundary (spending exactly the limit is meant to be allowed), leaves Remaining() reporting tokens that cannot be spent, and edits the boundary test to stop covering the exact-limit case; revert the comparison and the test change.

If the limit really has to be exclusive, that is an API change: update the Spend and Remaining docs, make Remaining return limit-spent-1, fix the error message, and explain it in the PR.

responses.note: Reverted the comparison in ledger.go Spend to `l.spent[tenant]+n > lim`, so the limit is inclusive again and matches the Spend doc comment, the ErrOverBudget doc, the '%d + %d > %d' error text and Remaining(). rereview.summary: Both earlier blocking comments are resolved: Spend uses `>` again so the limit is inclusive as documented (base..HEAD no longer touches ledger.go), and the tests now pin the boundary (exact-limit spend succeeds with remaining 0, limit+1 and one-past-limit are refused without changing the balance, limit 1 is spendable, the last reported token can be spent). go vet and go test -race pass.

comments.body: errors.New drops the error wrapping that fmt.Errorf gives you, so callers can no longer use errors.Is on this error. Keep fmt.Errorf here.

review.summary: Switching to errors.New loses error wrapping; revert to fmt.Errorf.

responses.note: fmt.Errorf only wraps when the format contains a %w verb and a matching error argument. The old call was fmt.Errorf("UPSTREAM_URL is required") with no %w and no arguments, so it returned a plain leaf error (a *fmt.wrapError is only made for %w). errors.Unwrap on it was nil and there was nothing for errors.Is to match except the value itself, and that is a fresh value on every call, so no caller could have matched it. errors.New gives the same message and the same empty unwrap chain, so behaviour does not change. The calls that do have a cause (UPSTREAM_URL parse error, UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT) still use fmt.Errorf with %w and are untouched. Added tests in config_test.go: TestLoadConfigMissingURLErrorIsLeaf checks the exact message, checks that errors.Unwrap is nil, and checks that the pre-PR fmt.Errorf form gives the same message and also unwraps to nil. TestLoadConfigBadTimeoutWrapsCause checks that the wrapped path still wraps its cause. go vet ./... and go test -race ./... pass.

reply.summary: Kept errors.New: the replaced fmt.Errorf had no %w, so it never wrapped anything and errors.Is behaviour is the same. Added tests that pin this (the message, a nil Unwrap, the pre-PR form matching) and that the %w paths still wrap their cause. vet and race tests pass.

rows.label: defect
rows.title: ledger: add Refund for cancelled completions

first_lines: oracle_refund_test.go:17: remaining after refunding more than was spent = 150, above the limit of 100

comments.body: Refund does no validation. It refunds more than the tenant has spent, so spent goes negative and Remaining() returns more than the limit: Spend 50 then Refund 500 gives Remaining 550 on a 100 limit, so the tenant can overspend its budget. A negative n raises spent without the limit check in Spend. An unknown tenant gets a spent entry. Make Refund return an error like Spend does: reject n <= 0, reject unknown tenants, and reject (or clamp, and document it) n > spent[tenant], so spent never drops below 0.

TestRefund only covers the happy path. Add cases for refunding more than was spent (Remaining must never exceed the limit), n <= 0, and an unknown tenant, so the bounds checks above are pinned. Also check the Spend error instead of discarding it with _.

r1.summary: Refund is unbounded: a refund larger than what was spent, or a negative one, breaks the ledger invariant 0 <= spent <= limit and can hand a tenant tokens beyond its limit. Add input validation and edge-case tests before merging.

comments.body: Refund validates nothing. A refund larger than what the tenant has spent drives spent[tenant] negative, so Remaining() goes above the limit and the tenant can then Spend more than its budget (e.g. Spend 50, Refund 200 -> Remaining 250 on a 100 limit). A negative n silently turns Refund into an unchecked spend that skips the limit check in Spend, and an unknown tenant gets a spent entry created. Make Refund return an error like Spend does: reject n <= 0, reject unknown tenants, and reject (or clamp to) n > spent[tenant], so spent never drops below 0.

TestRefund covers only the happy path and drops the Spend error with `_ =`. Add cases for refunding more than was spent (Remaining must not go above the limit), for n <= 0, and for an unknown tenant, and check the Spend error in the setup.

r2.summary: Refund has no bounds or input checks: over-refunds or negative refunds let a tenant exceed its token budget. Add validation with an error return, and tests for those cases.

comments.body: Refund subtracts n from spent with no validation. A refund larger than what the tenant has spent drives spent[tenant] below zero, so Remaining() returns more than the tenant's budget (e.g. Spend 50 then Refund 80 on a 100 budget gives Remaining 130), and a negative n silently charges the tenant instead. Retried or duplicated cancel handlers make this easy to hit and it lets a tenant exceed its quota. Reject n <= 0 and clamp/reject refunds above the current spent amount (return an error), and add tests for over-refund and non-positive n.

Refund for an unknown tenant creates a spent entry with a negative value, while Spend returns an error for unknown tenants (see TestSpendUnknownTenant). Refund should check the tenant exists and return an error like Spend does; change the signature to `Refund(tenant string, n int) error` so the handler can see failures, and test the unknown-tenant case.
The test discards the error from Spend (`_ = l.Spend(...)`); check it with t.Fatal so a failing setup isn't misreported as a Refund bug.

d1.summary: Refund has no bounds or tenant checks: over-refunds or negative amounts corrupt the ledger and let a tenant spend past its budget, and the unknown-tenant path differs from Spend. Add validation with an error return and tests for those cases.

responses.note: Refund now returns error. It rejects n <= 0 ('must be positive'), unknown tenants (no spent entry created), and n > spent[tenant] with the new sentinel ErrOverRefund (rejected, not clamped, documented in the doc comment); a rejected refund leaves the balance unchanged, so 0 <= spent <= limit holds and Remaining() never exceeds the limit.

TestRefund now checks the Spend and Refund errors and covers refunding exactly the spent amount (back to the limit). Added TestRefundMoreThanSpent (51 and 500 after spending 50, and 1 with nothing spent: errors.Is ErrOverRefund, Remaining unchanged and never above the limit), TestRefundRejectsNonPositive (0 and -5 rejected, balance unchanged, a later spend past the limit still gets ErrOverBudget), TestRefundUnknownTenant (error, no spent entry created).

reply.summary: Refund now validates its input and returns an error like Spend: n must be positive, the tenant must be known, and refunds above what was spent are rejected with ErrOverRefund, so the ledger invariant 0 <= spent <= limit holds. Edge-case tests added; go vet ./... and go test -race ./... pass.

rereview.summary: Both round-0 blocking comments are resolved: Refund now rejects n <= 0, unknown tenants (without creating a spent entry) and refunds above spent (ErrOverRefund, balance unchanged) under the mutex, so 0 <= spent <= limit holds; the new tests pin each case and check Spend/Refund errors. Refund has no other callers, so the signature change breaks nothing; go vet and go test -race pass.

rows.label: defect
rows.title: store: tidy the usage report query

first_lines: oracle_common_test.go:44: UsageQuery = "SELECT model, SUM(tokens) FROM usage WHERE tenant = $1 AND ts > $2 GROUP BY model ORDER BY model" [acme 2026-11-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC]; want ts >= $2 and the tenant as a parameter

comments.body: This is not a tidy-up: changing `ts >= $2` to `ts > $2` changes behaviour. The usage report now leaves out every row whose timestamp equals `since` exactly. Report windows usually start on a boundary such as midnight or the start of a billing period, so usage recorded at that instant drops out of every report: it is outside this window, and the previous window (ts < since) does not count it either. Tokens go uncounted. Restore `>=` (an inclusive lower bound with an exclusive upper bound is the usual half-open window). If an exclusive bound really is intended, say so in the PR and the doc comment, and explain how callers avoid the gap.

TestUsageQueryArgs only checks that the query is non-empty, which is why this boundary change passed CI. Assert the exact query text, or at least the `ts >= $2` predicate, and check that args[1] == since, so the window semantics are pinned by a test.

rows.label: defect
rows.title: upstream: close the response body next to the decode

first_lines: oracle_common_test.go:144: status 503: response body not closed
oracle_common_test.go:144: status 401: response body not closed

comments.body: Moving `defer resp.Body.Close()` below the status check means the non-200 path (line 45-47) now returns without ever closing the response body. It only reads up to 512 bytes and returns, so every upstream error (429, 5xx, 401...) leaks the body: the underlying TCP connection is never returned to the transport's pool and its read goroutines/file descriptors stay alive until the server closes it. Under an upstream outage or rate-limit storm this exhausts connections/FDs. Keep the defer immediately after the `err != nil` check on `u.HTTP.Do` (as on base), or explicitly close the body in the error branch. A regression test using an httptest server returning 500 plus a counting/wrapping RoundTripper (or checking the body's Close was called) would pin this.

r1.summary: The refactor is not behaviour-neutral: it stops closing the HTTP response body on non-200 responses, leaking connections on every upstream error. Restore the defer to right after the Do error check.

comments.body: Moving `defer resp.Body.Close()` below the status check means the non-200 path returns without ever closing resp.Body (it only reads up to 512 bytes via LimitReader). Every upstream error (429/5xx, exactly what happens under load) leaks the response body and its connection: the Transport cannot reuse or release it, so file descriptors and goroutines pile up until the gateway exhausts connections. The body must be closed on every path once Do returns err == nil. Put `defer resp.Body.Close()` back immediately after the `if err != nil` check following u.HTTP.Do (line 44), as on base. Add a test that triggers the error path repeatedly and checks that connections are closed or reused, for example with an httptest server's ConnState hook or a counting RoundTripper whose body records Close.

r2.summary: The PR is not a pure reordering: the non-200 error path no longer closes the response body, which leaks connections on every upstream error. Restore the defer directly after the Do error check.

comments.body: Moving `defer resp.Body.Close()` below the status check means the non-200 path (read up to 512 bytes, then return the error) never closes the response body. Every upstream error (429/5xx, which are exactly the bursty cases) leaks the body and its connection: the transport cannot reuse or free it, so file descriptors and goroutines pile up under error load. Keep the defer right after the `err != nil` check (as before), or close the body explicitly in the error branch. A test that counts closes with a wrapping RoundTripper/body on a non-200 response would catch this.

d1.summary: The move introduces a resource leak: the response body is no longer closed when upstream returns a non-200 status. Restore the defer right after the error check.

responses.note: Confirmed the leak: a new regression test, TestCompleteClosesBody, wraps the client's transport in a RoundTripper that counts bodies opened and closed. Against the PR as it stood, it reported 'closed 0 of 3 response bodies' for 401, 429 and 500. Fixed with your second option: the non-200 branch now calls resp.Body.Close() before it returns. The `defer resp.Body.Close()` stays next to the decode, as PR.md intends. The test covers 200, 200 with bad JSON, 401, 429 and 500 with a 4 KiB body (more than the 512-byte read limit), and checks that every body handed out is closed. `go vet ./... && go test -race ./...` passes.

reply.summary: The non-200 path now closes the response body explicitly, so connections go back to the pool on upstream errors. The defer stays beside the decode as the PR describes. Added TestCompleteClosesBody (counting RoundTripper, 5 cases) as the regression test. It failed before the fix and passes after it. vet and race tests are green.

The new TestCompleteClosesBody counts opened and closed bodies across 200, bad JSON, 401, 429 and 500; it fails on round0 (closed 0 of 3) and passes on HEAD, and vet and race tests are green.
